title: Social cost of carbon

definition.text: An estimate, usually in dollars, of the economic damage caused by emitting one more ton of carbon dioxide.

facts.text: By putting climate effects into money terms, it lets policymakers weigh actions that raise or cut greenhouse gas emissions.
It is widely used in regulatory impact analyses, cost-benefit assessments and climate policy.
Its roots lie in Arthur Pigou's 1912 proposal to tax activities that cause negative externalities such as pollution.
Estimates are very sensitive to a few assumptions, above all the discount rate, the damage function and climate sensitivity.
US values have swung from $6 per ton under Trump (7% discount rate) to over $51 per ton under Biden (3% rate).
The SCC is distinct from carbon pricing tools such as taxes or cap-and-trade, though it can inform them.
Some scholars argue its one-extra-ton logic is mismatched to the climate crisis, and that carbon budgets or caps may fit better.

contested_note: Economists, scientists and ethicists criticize the SCC for its sensitivity to assumptions, its ethics and its political volatility.

title: Calculating the social cost of carbon

definition.text: The chain of steps used to estimate the social cost of carbon, from projecting emissions to discounting future damages.

facts.text: The steps are: project future emissions, model the climate response, assess impacts, put a money value on damages, and discount them.
A low discount rate of 1–2% values future welfare nearly equal to today's; a high rate of 4–5% discounts future damages heavily.
Recent literature supports declining discount rates that start higher and fall over time.
Some versions add a catastrophic risk premium to account for possible disasters and society's dislike of risk.

title: DICE, FUND and PAGE models
article: Social cost of carbon#Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs)

definition.text: The three main integrated assessment models that have historically underpinned social cost of carbon estimates.

facts.text: DICE finds a single global optimal path and assumes damages grow with the square of temperature, without tipping points.
FUND models impacts by region and sector and allows some regions to gain from warming.
PAGE is probabilistic, using Monte Carlo simulations of thousands of futures and modelling catastrophic risks.
Their different methods can give dramatically different values; the Obama-era SCC averaged runs of all three.

title: Tipping points in the social cost of carbon

definition.text: Extensions to climate-economy models that add abrupt, irreversible damages when warming crosses critical thresholds.

facts.text: Standard models assume smooth, continuous damages, which may underestimate risk.
Modelling studies suggest that including tipping points can double the social cost of carbon.
One method adds a probability of a tipping event times its expected catastrophic damages.

title: Marginal abatement cost

definition.text: The cost of reducing pollution by one more unit.

facts.text: Marginal cost is the cost of one additional unit, so this measures the cost of the next unit of pollution cut.
It can be negative when the low-carbon option is cheaper than business as usual, but it often rises steeply as more pollution is cut.
A marginal abatement cost curve ranks reductions by their marginal cost.
Policymakers use the curves to see how much abatement is possible at what cost; carbon traders use them to model carbon prices.
Studies worldwide find that making buildings more energy efficient and replacing fossil power with renewables are usually the cheapest cuts.
The curves are criticized for poor transparency and weak treatment of uncertainty, timing, sector interactions and side benefits.

contested_note: The way marginal abatement cost curves are built and used to choose measures has been criticized.

definition.text: Weitzman's result on whether a price control (such as a tax) or a quantity control (such as a cap) works better when costs are uncertain.

facts.text: The choice depends on the relative slopes of marginal costs and marginal damages from pollution.
If marginal costs are steeper, price controls are more effective; if marginal damages are steeper, quantity controls are.

title: Martin Weitzman

definition.text: An American economist at Harvard whose research centred on environmental economics, especially climate change and catastrophes.

facts.text: He added the risk of dramatic climate change to cost-benefit analysis to argue for immediate action.
He argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails that standard models handle poorly.
He showed when price controls beat quantity controls under uncertainty.
He co-wrote Climate Shock (2015) with Gernot Wagner.

title: DICE model

definition.text: William Nordhaus's integrated assessment model that combines economics, the carbon cycle, climate science and impacts to weigh the costs and benefits of slowing climate change.

facts.text: Nordhaus first proposed it in a 1992 Cowles Foundation discussion paper; a regional variant, RICE, followed in 1996.
It is one of three main models the US Environmental Protection Agency uses to estimate the social cost of carbon.
Its central assumption is that externalities create costs missing from prices, which government must add.
It uses the market return on capital, around 4% on average, as its discount rate.
In 2020, a rerun with updated science and discount rates found the optimal goal was below 2.0 °C of warming, not the 3.5 °C Nordhaus first found.
A 2020 paper with an updated damage function found warming of around 2 °C would be optimal, depending on climate sensitivity.
It treats innovation as external; a variant with induced technical change favours strong early investment in mitigation.
Critics have attacked its sensitivity to assumptions and its choice of discount rate.

contested_note: The model's damage function and discount rate are disputed by critics, and a 2020 rerun changed its optimal warming goal.
